text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thank you for reaching out, C. I'm sorry about your dad. I will help the three of you work toward a plan, but I cannot make legal decisions or move money. To start, I will keep a shared list of everyone's needs, concerns and expectations (I'll call them NCEs). From your message, I have noted two for you: you do not agree to a "family discount" sale to A and her husband, and you want B's need for money to be considered. Is that right? What else matters to you, for example a fair price, timing, or keeping the house in the family? Also, what does the will say about how the house is split?

Not quite: I want a fair financial share, and I haven’t agreed to a discounted sale. B’s needs should be heard, but I don’t know that she needs money. A fair price matters; there’s no real rush. I’m not sure what the will says about the split.

Hello A. I'm sorry about your dad. C asked me to help the three of you plan what to do with the house. I cannot make legal decisions or move money. I am keeping a shared list of each person's needs, concerns and expectations (NCEs). I understand you and your husband would like to buy the house. What matters most to you here, and what price or terms did you have in mind? Please tell me if I have anything wrong.
I’d like to buy the house with my husband at a family discount. We haven’t settled on a price or terms, and C’s agreement is needed; she hasn’t agreed yet.

Hello B. I'm sorry about your dad. C asked me to help the three of you plan what to do with the house. I cannot make legal decisions or move money. I am keeping a shared list of each person's needs, concerns and expectations (NCEs). What matters most to you about the house and the will? C mentioned money may be a concern for you, but I would rather hear it from you. Please correct anything I have wrong.

Thank you. Yes, money is a concern—I’d like to use my share to start a dance studio. I don’t know what the house is worth or what the will means for each of us, so I’m not sure what amount might be possible. I’d like that included in the list.

Thank you, C, and I've corrected my note. Here is the draft list I'm sharing with all three of you. Please tell me what is wrong or missing.

C: wants a fair financial share. Has not agreed to a discounted sale. Wants a fair price. Feels no rush. Thinks B's needs should be heard, but in B's own words.
A: wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount. No price or terms yet. Knows C's agreement is needed.
B: wants to use her share to start a dance studio. Does not know the house's value or what the will gives each sister.
Mine: no one yet knows what the will says or what the house is worth. I suggest these two facts come before any talk of price. I cannot read the will for you or give legal advice.

Suggested next steps: one of you asks the executor or the lawyer handling the estate to explain the split. The three of you then agree on one independent appraiser. Would you support those steps?

I support finding out what the will says and agreeing on an independent appraiser. I can’t confirm A knows my agreement is needed. Please note that I won’t subsidize a discounted purchase; I want a fair financial share. No rush from me.

Thank you, A. Here is the draft list I'm sharing with all three of you. Please tell me what is wrong or missing.

A: wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount. No price or terms yet. Knows C's agreement is needed.
C: wants a fair financial share. Has not agreed to a discounted sale. Wants a fair price. Feels no rush.
B: wants to use her share to start a dance studio. Does not know the house's value or what the will gives each sister.
Mine: no one yet knows what the will says or what the house is worth. I suggest these two facts come before any talk of price. I cannot read the will for you or give legal advice.

Two questions for you. Would you support asking the executor or estate lawyer to explain the split, and then choosing one independent appraiser together? And what would a "family discount" mean to you, and why does it matter to you?

Yes, I’d support clarifying the will and choosing an independent appraiser together. By a family discount, I mean a price below the appraised value; we haven’t decided how much below. It matters because buying the house would help me build financial independence with my husband.

Thank you, B. I've added your point. Here is the draft list I'm sharing with all three of you. Please tell me what is wrong or missing.

B: wants to use her share to start a dance studio. Does not know the house's value or what the will gives each sister.
A: wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount. No price or terms yet. Knows C's agreement is needed.
C: wants a fair financial share. Has not agreed to a discounted sale. Wants a fair price. Feels no rush.
Mine: no one yet knows what the will says or what the house is worth. I suggest these two facts come before any talk of price. I cannot read the will for you or give legal advice.

Would you support asking the executor or estate lawyer to explain the split, and then choosing one independent appraiser together? Also, do you have a timeline for the studio?
Yes, that seems sensible. I don’t have a set timeline for the studio, but I’d like to move forward when we know what funds may be available.

Thank you, A. All three of you now agree on two first steps: ask the executor or estate lawyer to explain the split, then choose one independent appraiser together.

I've updated the list. C added that she will not pay for a discount out of her share. B has no fixed timeline but wants to know what funds may be available. Your NCE now reads: wants to buy the house with her husband to build financial independence, ideally below the appraised value.

Here are some options to test against the list. Please say which ones you could live with, and feel free to reject any.
One: you buy at the appraised value, and your own share counts toward the price.
Two: you buy at the appraised value, with extra time or staged payments in place of a lower price.
Three: any discount comes only out of your own share, so C and B still receive their full shares.
Four: the house sells on the open market, and each sister gets her share.
My own view: options one to three seem to fit everyone's NCEs best. Option four is a fallback. Please tell me if you see it differently.

I could consider options one or two, depending on the figures and terms. I’m open to option three only if it’s legally workable and the numbers are clear. I’d prefer to buy the house, so option four would be a fallback, not my choice. I can’t yet say which option works best for everyone.

Thank you, C. I've added your point that you will not pay for a discount out of your share. I've also changed A's line, since you can't confirm she knows your agreement is needed.

All three of you agree on the first steps: ask the executor or estate lawyer to explain the split, then choose one independent appraiser together. A explained that a "family discount" means a price below the appraised value. She wants the house to build financial independence with her husband. B has no fixed timeline but wants to know what funds may be available.

Here are some options to test against the list. Please say which ones you could live with, and feel free to reject any.
One: A buys at the appraised value, and her own share counts toward the price.
Two: A buys at the appraised value, with extra time or staged payments in place of a lower price.
Three: the house sells on the open market, and each sister gets her share.
My view: option one or two seems to fit everyone's NCEs. Option three is a fallback. Please tell me if you disagree.

Option one could work, once we know the will’s split and the appraisal. I’m not agreeing to staged payments without clear terms that protect my share. Option three is acceptable if A can’t buy at a fair price. There’s no need to rush.

Thank you, B. All three of you agree on the first steps: ask the executor or estate lawyer to explain the split, then choose one independent appraiser together.

Here is where the options stand. Please say which ones you could live with.
One: A buys at the appraised value, and her own share counts toward the price. A and C are both open to this.
Two: A pays over time instead of all at once. A is open to this. C would need clear terms that protect her share.
Three: any discount comes only out of A's own share. A is open to this if it is legally workable.
Four: the house sells on the open market, and each sister gets her share. A and C both see this as a fallback.
One question for you: under options two and three, would waiting for your full share, or getting it in parts, affect your plans for the studio?

I could live with option one if my share is paid out clearly; option four could also work. Under option two, getting my share in parts would make planning for the studio harder, so I’d need clear timing. Option three might be workable if any discount doesn’t reduce my share, but that needs to be confirmed.

Thank you, A. Here is where all three of you stand. Option one has support from everyone: you buy at the appraised value, and your own share counts toward the price. B and C both want their shares paid out clearly. C will not accept staged payments without clear terms that protect her share. B would need clear timing for any staged payments. Open-market sale is everyone's fallback.

Proposed plan: first, the executor or estate lawyer explains the split. Second, the three of you choose one independent appraiser. Third, you check whether you can buy at that value using your share. If not, the house goes to open-market sale. Any discount out of your own share stays open, pending legal advice.

Does this plan work for you? Please say so if it does not.
Yes, that plan works for me, subject to confirming the will, appraisal, and whether I can finance the purchase at that value. Any discount from my share can stay open pending legal advice.

Thank you, C. Option one has support from all three of you: A buys at the appraised value, and her own share counts toward the price. B wants her share paid out clearly. She would need clear timing for any staged payments. Open-market sale is everyone's fallback.

Proposed plan: first, the executor or estate lawyer explains the split. Second, the three of you choose one independent appraiser. Third, A checks whether she can buy at that value using her share. If not, the house goes to open-market sale. Staged payments happen only with clear terms that protect your share and B's. Any discount comes only from A's own share and is subject to legal advice.

Does this plan work for you? Please say so if it does not.

It works, provided any discount comes solely from A’s share and doesn’t reduce mine or B’s. We should confirm the will and appraisal first. Any staged payments need clear terms protecting both our shares.

Thank you, B. Option one has support from all three of you: A buys at the appraised value, and her own share counts toward the price.

Proposed plan: first, the executor or estate lawyer explains the split. Second, the three of you choose one independent appraiser. Third, A checks whether she can buy at that value using her share. If not, the house goes to open-market sale. Staged payments happen only with clear terms and timing that protect your share and C's. Any discount comes only from A's own share and is subject to legal advice.

Does this plan work for you? Please say so if it does not.
Yes, that plan works for me, as long as my share and any payment timing are clearly confirmed.
